title: Bayesian Statistics
short: Bayesian Statistics explores a key idea, method or development within statistics & probability.
description: Bayesian Statistics explores a key idea, method or development within statistics & probability. Its history, evidence and applications connect this field to wider scientific, historical and cultural questions.

title: Propositional Logic
short: Propositional Logic explores a key idea, method or development within mathematical logic.
description: Propositional Logic explores a key idea, method or development within mathematical logic. Its history, evidence and applications connect this field to wider scientific, historical and cultural questions.

title: Predicate Logic
short: Predicate Logic explores a key idea, method or development within mathematical logic.
description: Predicate Logic explores a key idea, method or development within mathematical logic. Its history, evidence and applications connect this field to wider scientific, historical and cultural questions.

title: Quantum Mechanics (Quantum Physics)
short: The physical theory used to describe matter and radiation at atomic and subatomic scales.
description: Quantum mechanics describes physical systems at scales where classical concepts alone do not correctly predict observations. Its mathematical framework uses quantum states, operators and probabilities to calculate possible measurement outcomes. Experiments reveal phenomena such as quantized energy levels, wave-particle behaviour, interference and uncertainty relations. Quantum mechanics is essential to understanding atoms, chemical bonds, semiconductors, lasers, magnetic resonance and modern particle physics.

title: Quantum Entanglement
short: A quantum relationship in which a combined system cannot be fully described as independent states of its parts.
description: Quantum entanglement occurs when the state of a composite quantum system cannot be represented as a product of separate states for its components. Measurements on separated parts can show correlations stronger than any allowed by classical local-hidden-variable models, as tested through Bell inequalities. Entanglement does not provide a way to send controllable information faster than light. It is studied as a resource in quantum communication, sensing and computation.

title: Standard Model
short: The tested theoretical framework describing known elementary particles and three fundamental interactions.
description: The Standard Model of particle physics organizes elementary matter particles into quarks and leptons and describes their interactions through the electromagnetic, weak and strong forces. Force-carrying particles include photons, gluons and W and Z bosons; the Higgs field and Higgs boson are part of the model's account of mass generation for elementary particles. The model has passed extensive experimental tests, but it does not include gravity and does not explain every observation, including dark matter.

title: Entropy
short: A thermodynamic state quantity connected to energy dispersal and the number of microscopic arrangements compatible with a system's macroscopic state.
description: Entropy is a central concept in thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. In classical thermodynamics, changes in entropy constrain which processes can occur spontaneously and express the second law: the total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. In statistical mechanics, entropy is related to the number of microscopic configurations consistent with a macroscopic description. It is not simply a synonym for disorder; its meaning depends on the physical model and the information being considered.

title: Heat Transfer

title: Electromagnetism
short: The physical interaction involving electric and magnetic fields and their effects on charged matter and electromagnetic radiation.
description: Electromagnetism unifies electricity and magnetism in a framework describing electric charges, currents and fields. Maxwell's equations explain how changing electric and magnetic fields are related and predict electromagnetic waves, including radio waves, visible light, X-rays and other parts of the spectrum. Electromagnetic theory underpins electric motors, generators, antennas, optical technologies and modern communications. It is also one of the fundamental interactions represented in the Standard Model.

title: Laser
short: A device that produces light through stimulated emission, typically in a narrow and coherent beam.
description: A laser amplifies light by stimulated emission of radiation. A gain medium is supplied with energy to create a population inversion, and an optical resonator helps build up selected modes of light. Laser output can be highly directional, coherent and concentrated in wavelength, although real devices vary widely in pulse duration, spectrum and power. Lasers are used in telecommunications, medicine, manufacturing, measurement, scientific instruments and consumer electronics.

title: Isotopes
short: Atoms of the same chemical element that have equal proton numbers but different neutron numbers.
description: Isotopes are forms of an element whose atoms contain the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They therefore share the same atomic number but have different mass numbers. Isotopes of an element usually have very similar chemical behaviour, while their nuclear stability and radioactive properties can differ. Isotope science is important in nuclear physics, radiometric dating, medicine, environmental tracing and understanding the origin of elements.

title: Cell Membrane
short: A selectively permeable boundary that separates a cell from its surroundings and organizes exchange and communication.
description: Cell membranes are dynamic boundaries built mainly from a phospholipid bilayer with embedded or associated proteins, cholesterol in many eukaryotic membranes, and surface carbohydrates. Their selective permeability helps regulate the movement of ions and molecules, while membrane proteins support transport, signalling, recognition and adhesion. The fluid-mosaic model describes membranes as flexible structures whose components can move and interact, rather than rigid walls.

title: Mitochondria
short: Membrane-bound organelles that carry out major stages of aerobic energy conversion in most eukaryotic cells.
description: Mitochondria are organelles enclosed by outer and inner membranes. The inner membrane folds into cristae and contains components of the electron-transport chain and ATP synthase, which use a proton gradient to support ATP production during oxidative phosphorylation. Mitochondria also participate in metabolism, cell signalling and regulated cell death. They contain their own DNA, but most mitochondrial proteins are encoded by nuclear genes and imported into the organelle.

title: Bacteria
short: A diverse domain of single-celled prokaryotic organisms with major roles in ecosystems, health and industry.
description: Bacteria are prokaryotic microorganisms whose cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Most have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA concentrated in a nucleoid; many also have a peptidoglycan cell wall. Bacteria occur in nearly every environment and show enormous metabolic and ecological diversity. Many are harmless or beneficial, contributing to nutrient cycles, digestion and food production, while a smaller subset can cause disease.

title: Viruses
short: Acellular infectious agents that replicate by using the molecular machinery of host cells.
description: Viruses contain genetic material, either DNA or RNA, enclosed in a protein capsid and sometimes surrounded by a lipid envelope. They do not have the cellular machinery needed for independent reproduction or metabolism, so replication depends on infecting a host cell. Viruses infect organisms across all domains of life. Their diversity, evolution and interactions with hosts are central to medicine, ecology and molecular biology; whether viruses count as living remains a question of definition.

title: Plate Tectonics (Geology)
short: The scientific theory that Earth's outer rigid shell is divided into moving tectonic plates.
description: Plate tectonics explains the large-scale movement of Earth's lithosphere, which is divided into plates that interact at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries. Their motion is associated with seafloor spreading, subduction, mountain building, earthquakes and much volcanic activity. The modern theory developed through evidence including the fit of continents, fossil and rock distributions, seafloor mapping and magnetic patterns in oceanic crust. Plates move over geological time, while the mantle beneath them remains mostly solid and can deform slowly.

title: Earth's Atmosphere
short: The envelope of gases surrounding Earth, shaped by gravity and structured into layers with changing temperature and composition.
description: Earth's atmosphere is a mixture of gases held by gravity, together with variable water vapour and suspended particles. Dry air near the surface is dominated by nitrogen and oxygen, with argon and trace gases including carbon dioxide. Temperature-based layers include the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere. The atmosphere supports life, moderates energy exchange, drives weather and climate, and filters some harmful solar radiation. Its composition and structure vary with altitude, location and time.

title: The Water Cycle
short: The continuous movement and storage of water among the atmosphere, oceans, land, ice and underground reservoirs.
description: The water cycle describes exchanges of water among the atmosphere, surface waters, living things, ice and groundwater. Solar energy drives evaporation and transpiration, while cooling supports condensation and precipitation; gravity moves water through runoff, rivers and groundwater flow. The cycle is not a simple closed loop with one fixed route: water can be stored for very different lengths of time in oceans, glaciers, soils and aquifers. Human water use, land-use change and climate change alter parts of the cycle.

title: Disease Transmission
short: The processes through which infectious agents move between hosts or from environmental sources to people.
description: Disease transmission describes how an infectious agent moves from a reservoir or source to a susceptible host. Routes include direct contact, indirect contact through contaminated objects, respiratory particles, contaminated food or water, blood exposure and vectors such as mosquitoes. The importance of each route depends on the pathogen and context. Understanding transmission helps guide prevention measures such as ventilation, sanitation, vaccination, protective equipment and vector control.

title: Outbreak Investigation
short: A field epidemiology process used to identify the cause, source and spread of an unusual cluster of health events and guide control.
description: Outbreak investigation is a structured public-health response to an unexpected increase in disease or other health events. Investigators verify the diagnosis and whether an outbreak exists, define and find cases, describe patterns by time, place and person, develop and test hypotheses, and implement control measures. The sequence is adapted to urgency and available evidence; action to protect health may begin before every uncertainty is resolved. Communication with affected communities is central.

title: Sorting Algorithms
short: Algorithms that arrange a collection of items according to a specified ordering rule.
description: Sorting algorithms transform an unordered or partially ordered collection into a sequence that follows a chosen comparison or key. Common methods include insertion sort, merge sort, quicksort, heapsort and counting-based approaches. They differ in time and space requirements, stability, memory use and behaviour on particular input patterns. Sorting is a foundational computational task because ordered data can make searching, reporting, deduplication and later processing more efficient.

title: Graph Theory
short: The mathematical study of networks represented by vertices and edges.
description: Graph theory studies structures made of vertices, also called nodes, connected by edges. Graphs can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and may represent roads, social relationships, communication networks, dependencies or molecular structures. Core concepts include paths, cycles, connectivity, trees, matchings and graph colouring. Graph algorithms support route planning, network analysis, scheduling, recommendation systems and many other computational tasks.

title: Compiler
short: A program that translates or transforms source code into another representation while checking and preserving its intended meaning.
description: A compiler processes a program through stages that commonly include lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, intermediate representation, optimization and code generation. Some compilers translate to machine code, while others produce bytecode or another intermediate form. Compiler design balances correctness, performance, portability and diagnostics. Modern language implementations may combine compilation with interpretation and just-in-time compilation, so the boundary between a compiler and a runtime system is not always a simple one.

title: Encryption
short: The transformation of readable information into a protected form using a cryptographic method and key.
description: Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext so that information can be read only by parties with the appropriate decryption capability. Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret key, while public-key cryptography uses mathematically related public and private keys for different functions. Secure systems depend not only on algorithms but also on sound protocols, key management, implementation and operational practices. AES is a widely standardized symmetric block cipher; encryption alone does not guarantee authenticity or protect against every attack.

Keys and integrity constraints help express identity and relationships, while relational algebra provides a foundation for operations such as selection, projection and joins. SQL is widely used to define, query and manipulate relational databases. Practical database systems add indexing, transactions, concurrency control, recovery and query optimization to support reliable multi-user applications.

title: Set theory

title: Prime factorization
short: The expression of a whole number greater than one as a product of prime numbers.
description: Prime factorization breaks a composite integer into prime factors, which are numbers greater than one divisible only by one and themselves. title: Group theory

title: Vaccine immunology
short: The study of immune responses generated by vaccination, including antibodies, cellular immunity and immune memory.
description: Vaccine immunology studies how vaccines activate and shape the immune system. Vaccine antigens are recognized by immune cells, leading to responses that can include antibodies, helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells and long-lived memory cells. Different vaccine platforms stimulate these pathways in different ways, and protection varies by pathogen, vaccine, population and outcome. Vaccination can reduce the risk or severity of disease, but no vaccine is universally or perfectly protective.

title: Antimicrobial resistance
short: The ability of microorganisms to survive or grow despite medicines designed to kill them or stop their growth.
description: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites evolve or acquire mechanisms that reduce the effectiveness of medicines used against them. Resistance can emerge naturally, but inappropriate use of antimicrobials and weak infection prevention can accelerate its spread. It threatens routine treatment and modern medical procedures and requires coordinated action across human health, animal health, agriculture and the environment.

title: Clinical trials
short: Research studies involving people that assess the safety, effectiveness or other effects of health interventions.
description: Clinical trials are planned studies involving human participants that evaluate health-related interventions, including medicines, vaccines, devices, procedures and behavioural approaches. Their design may compare an intervention with placebo, usual care or another treatment. Many drug-development programmes use phases to study safety, dosage and effectiveness, but not every clinical study follows the same phase sequence. Ethical review, informed consent, transparent registration and careful analysis are essential.

title: Evidence-based medicine
short: An approach to clinical decision-making that combines research evidence, professional expertise and patient values.
description: Evidence-based medicine integrates the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the values and circumstances of individual patients. It does not mean following a single study or treating guidelines as automatic rules. Systematic reviews can synthesize multiple studies, but their conclusions depend on the quality, relevance and certainty of the underlying evidence. Good decisions also consider harms, benefits, feasibility and patient preferences.

title: Global health
short: A field of research, policy and practice focused on improving health and equity across populations and countries.
description: Global health addresses health challenges that cross borders and are shaped by social, economic, political and environmental systems. It combines research, policy and practice, with attention to health equity, prevention, health systems, international cooperation and the conditions that shape population health. It is broader than responding to outbreaks: it includes chronic disease, maternal and child health, environmental risks, access to care and the distribution of resources and power.

title: Climate science
short: The scientific study of Earth's climate system, its variability, drivers and long-term changes.
description: Climate science examines the long-term patterns and drivers of Earth's climate system, including the atmosphere, oceans, land, ice and living systems. Evidence comes from instrumental measurements, satellites, ice cores, tree rings, sediments and physical theory. Climate varies naturally, but multiple independent lines of evidence show that recent global warming is primarily driven by human activities, especially greenhouse-gas emissions. Climate science distinguishes long-term climate trends from short-term weather.

title: Climate modelling
short: Computer-based representations of the climate system used to understand past change and explore possible future climates.
description: Climate models are numerical representations of interactions among the atmosphere, ocean, land, ice and other parts of the climate system. They apply physical laws and parameterizations to simulate climate behaviour under specified conditions and scenarios. Models are evaluated against observations and past climates, and their strengths differ by variable, region and timescale. Projections are conditional estimates, not exact forecasts of the weather on a particular future date.
